questions.q: Name the two supporting characters who physically appear on stage in "On the Face of It" and state one key difference in how each responds to Derry's burned face.
questions.a: The two supporting characters who appear on stage are Mr. Lamb (Scene One and Three) and Derry's mother (Scene Two). Mr. Lamb acknowledges the burn matter-of-factly ("I should say... you got burned in a fire") but immediately reframes it as unimportant compared to shared humanity ("You've got a burned face, I've got a tin leg. Not important"). Derry's mother never mentions the face directly but acts out of fear and overprotection, forbidding Derry from returning to Mr. Lamb ("you're not to go back there"). A wrong answer that lists "the woman at the bus stop" or "kids who call him Lamey-Lamb" as on-stage characters reveals confusion between reported speech and dramatic presence.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Mr. Lamb's "weed garden" speech (comparing weeds to flowers) functions as a direct counter-argument to Derry's belief that his burned face makes him fundamentally different and unlovable.
questions.a: Mr. Lamb's weed garden speech establishes that labels like "weed" vs "flower" are arbitrary human judgments, not inherent qualities — "Why is one green, growing plant called a weed and another 'flower'? Where's the difference. It's all life... growing. Same as you and me." This directly counters Derry's fixed belief that his burned face makes him a "monstrous beast" who "won't change" and "no one'll kiss me ever." By equating weeds and flowers as equally valid "life," Mr. Lamb argues that Derry's disfigurement is just a label society imposes, not a definition of his worth. A wrong answer that merely summarizes the speech without linking it to Derry's "Beauty and the Beast" reference shows the student cannot connect textual evidence to character psychology.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "dramatic foil" to analyze how Derry's mother functions as a foil to Mr. Lamb in Scene Two. Use one specific line from each character to support your analysis.
questions.a: A dramatic foil contrasts with another character to highlight the latter's traits. Derry's mother foils Mr. Lamb: where Mr. Lamb says "The gate's always open" (inviting risk, choice, world), the mother says "You'll stop here" (enforcing safety, control, isolation). Mr. Lamb tells Derry "You could get on better than all the rest" (agency, potential); the mother says "You're best off here" (resignation, limitation). Mr. Lamb's "Everything's yours if you want it" (expansive) contrasts with the mother's "I know what there is to know and you're not to go back there" (restrictive). A wrong answer that only describes their personalities without using the term "foil" or quoting lines shows inability to apply literary terminology to textual analysis.

questions.q: Analyze how the off-stage characters (the woman at the bus stop, the "young lads" who scrump apples, the kids who chant "Lamey-Lamb") collectively construct the social world that Derry and Mr. Lamb react against. What pattern do their behaviors reveal about society's treatment of difference?
questions.a: These off-stage voices form a chorus of societal judgment: the bus-stop woman reduces Derry to "a face only a mother could love" (pity disguised as cruelty); the "young lads" steal apples but Mr. Lamb notes "You're not so young" — implying Derry is prematurely aged by trauma; the "Lamey-Lamb" chant shows children mock disability casually. The pattern: society either pities (mother, bus-stop woman), mocks (kids), or ignores (lads stealing) difference — never engages with the person. Derry internalizes this ("People are afraid of me"); Mr. Lamb externalizes it ("They get tired of it, in the end"). A wrong answer that treats these as unrelated anecdotes misses the structural point: Hill uses reported voices to build the hostile social context without crowding the stage.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument that Mr. Lamb's death in Scene Three is narratively necessary for Derry's transformation. Could Derry have changed without this loss? Justify using the play's final dialogue.
questions.a: Mr. Lamb's death is narratively necessary because it forces Derry to convert Mr. Lamb's philosophy from external guidance into internal ownership. While alive, Mr. Lamb is a crutch — Derry says "I'll come back. You see. You wait." The death removes the safety net: Derry returns to an empty garden, kneels, and weeps "Lamey-Lamb. I did... come back" — claiming the name the world uses mockingly as his own term of endearment. The final line "They never do, though. Not them. Never do come back" (Mr. Lamb's expectation) is proven wrong by Derry's return. Without death, Derry might have remained a visitor; with it, he becomes the heir. A wrong answer that calls the death "sad" or "unnecessary" fails to evaluate structural function — it treats plot as event, not design.

questions.q: Create an alternative ending for Scene Three where Mr. Lamb survives the fall. Write 4-5 lines of dialogue showing how Derry's first words to a living Mr. Lamb would demonstrate that his transformation is complete.
questions.a:
A strong answer shows Derry initiating the relationship on equal terms, not as a grateful recipient. Example:
DERRE: (breathless) You're heavy for an old man. Give me your arm — I'll haul you up.
MR LAMB: (grinning) Bossy, aren't you? "Give me your arm." Since when do you give orders?
DERRE: Since I decided this garden needs two people to run it. The bees, the apples, the jelly — and the gate.
MR LAMB: The gate's always been open.
DERRE: Good. Then I don't need to climb the wall anymore. I'll use the gate. Like a friend.
This demonstrates: physical agency (hauling him up), verbal confidence (banter), ownership ("this garden needs two people"), and symbolic shift from wall-climbing (hiding) to gate-using (belonging). A weak answer has Derry thanking Mr. Lamb or apologizing — showing dependence, not transformation.
